Thank you. Honourable Minister and Madam Chair, I will now handle issues relating to children with disabilities. Uganda has a legal framework specifically protecting children with disabilities. The Persons with Disabilities Act, CAP 115, provides that a child with a disability enjoys all rights under the Children Act on an equal basis with other children and should not be separated from their family except in accordance with the law and the child's best interests. The Act also places obligations on educational institutions to provide inclusive education, make structural adjustments for accessibility and for government-aided institutions, provide sign language services, appropriate learning materials and assistive devices. It also requires schools to facilitate participation in sports and co-curricular activities. Uganda has made progress in enrolling learners with disabilities within the education system, including through inclusive education. However, we acknowledge that enrolment does not necessarily mean effective inclusion. and we continue to face challenges relating to accessibility of schools, assistive devices, specialized learning materials, trained personnel, and reasonable accommodation. The government is therefore focusing not only on getting children with disabilities into school, but also on ensuring retention, participation, and completion. Government is working to improve disability-friendly infrastructure and the provision of appropriate learning materials and assistive devices. Government is also strengthening early identification of development difficulties and disabilities. In collaboration with partners, Uganda has been assessing how developmental screening can be integrated into existing child health services so that children can be identified earlier and referred for appropriate intervention. Uganda also recognizes that disability can impose significant additional costs on families, including costs of transport, healthcare, assistive devices, and education. A significant recent development is the approval of the 15.6 billion in the financial year 2026-2027 national budget for the National Child Disability Assistance Program. The program is intended to provide predictable, predictable support to families caring for children with severe disabilities. This represents an important step towards strengthening social protection for children with disabilities and their families. Uganda recognizes that legal protection alone is not enough. The government is therefore working with communities, schools, health services, organizations of persons with disabilities and development partners to strengthen awareness Early identification, referral and inclusion. The legal position is that disability is not in itself enough. The legal position is that disability is not in itself a basis for separating child from his or her family. The Persons with Disabilities Act expressly protects the child's right to know and be cared for by their parents and/or guardian. Any separation must be in accordance with the law and the best interest of the child. In respect to inclusive education versus special schools, Uganda's legal framework promotes inclusive education. At the same time, we recognize that specialized services and specialized institutions continue to play a role for children with particular support needs. The objective is to ensure that specialized support complements inclusion rather than becoming a basis for unnecessary segregation. I beg to submit.

The Constitution of the Republic of Uganda sets the age of 18 as the minimum age of marriage for both men and women. There is no legal exception permitting child marriage on customary, religious, or other grounds, and any custom purporting to allow a marriage below 18 is unconstitutional and cannot prevail. In the constitutional petition case of Aboneka Michael and Kyria Martins versus the Attorney General, the Constitutional Court declared unconstitutional the provisions of the Customary Marriage Registration Act, the Marriage and Divorce of Mohammedans Act, and the Hindu Marriage and Divorce Act that permitted girls aged between 16 17 to get married. First, on food ration cuts, funding shortfalls have forced agencies like the World Food Program to drastically slash food rations, leaving a majority of refugee households severely food insecure. Secondly, basic services have been strained. Acute deficits have affected health care, water access, and sanitation, causing spikes in malnutrition and forcing children out of school in refugee settlements. Thirdly, environmental and land pressures. Rapidly growing populations have exhausted available land that has been provided for subsistence farming, aggravating land scarcity and intensifying local resource competition. Fourthly, tensions within host communities. Declining aid and support that fails to benefit surrounding local communities risk eroding the historical goodwill and hospitality of communities. And fifthly, the total cut down on support has impacted on durable solutions. Families that expect to be reintegrated with their families outside Uganda continue to be frustrated, and some of this is vented in several ways. Therefore, severe resource shortages, sustained high numbers of arrivals, and a prolonged failure of international responsibility sharing has trickled down and frustrating refugees. Would anyone be surprised that refugees resort to extreme measures? It's important that together we address the root cause of the problem. As far as psychological support is concerned, nonetheless, Counseling and therapy is provided where government of Uganda is working with key international and local actors such as UNHCR. With regard to questions on housing and homelessness, the government of Uganda reiterates its unwavering commitment to safeguarding the rights, dignity, and well-being of all children in accordance with the Constitution, the Children's Act as amended, and Uganda's obligations under the Convention on the Rights of the Child, as well as the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child. Uganda recognizes that adequate housing and protection from homelessness are essential components of a child's right to survival, development, and participation. Ensuring that every child grows up in a safe, stable, and nurturing environment remains a national priority. The government of Uganda has established legal, policy, and pragmatic measures to safeguard children's rights to adequate housing, security of tenure, and protection from forced evictions. These measures are implemented through national legislation, child protection systems, land governance frameworks, and emergency response mechanisms. The Uganda's National Housing Policy 2016 is the country's primary framework for ensuring access to adequate, safe, and affordable housing for all Ugandans. Grounded in constitutional commitments to decent shelter, the policy outlines the national housing deficit, key challenges, and the strategic interventions to guide government, private sector, and community action. The National Land Policy 2013 and the Land Act promote tenure, security, and require consultation, compensation, and resettlement before lawful eviction. Uganda's eviction and resettlement guidelines include child-specific protections. For children displaced by eviction, conflict, or disaster, compensation, temporary shelters, foster care, and kinship care options are provided. The Government has taken significant steps to strengthen child protection systems and reduce vulnerability to homelessness. Community-based child protection structures have been expanded to identify and support children at risk of family separation or street-connected living. The Government continues to work with local authorities and civil society to rehabilitate and reintegrate street-connected children, prioritizing family-based care over institutionalization. Uganda is scaling up social protection programs, including SAGE, and livelihood support initiatives to reduce household vulnerability and prevent child homelessness. Collaboration with development partners has strengthened alternative care frameworks, including foster care, kinship care, ensuring that children without parental care receive protection in family-like settings. Uganda acknowledges that urbanization, poverty, climate shocks, and family breakdown continue to place pressure on vulnerable households. The Ministry of Gender estimates that about 15,000 to 20,000 children are living or working on streets in major urban centers, with Kampala accounting for the largest share. The government of Uganda, through the Kampala City Authority, is currently undertaking slum upgrading programs to improve housing conditions for families with children. Uganda remains steadfast in its commitment to ensuring that no child is left without shelter, protection, or care. The government will continue working with all partners to uphold children's rights, strengthen family resilience, and build a society where every child grows up in safety and dignity. I thank you, Chair.

In the Ugandan legal framework, it allows children to be incarcerated with their mothers for a specific period of time, which is 18 to 24 months. Uganda recognizes that a child should not be deprived of liberty or punished because of an offense committed by his or her parent. The law and prison practice provide for young children to remain with their mothers in prison for a limited time, subject to the applicable legal framework. The child is treated as a child requiring care and protection and not as a prisoner. The child is therefore not subjected to the same regime as an incarcerated adult. During this period that a child remains with an incarcerated mother, the Uganda Prison Service provides for the child's basic needs, including accommodation, food, health care, and other essential care, while taking into account the child's age and developmental needs. The government also recognizes the importance of ensuring that children do not remain in prison beyond the period permitted by the law. Where a child reaches the prescribed age or where continued residence with a mother is no longer in the child's best interest, appropriate alternative care arrangements are made. These arrangements prioritize family-based care and the preservation of the child's family relationship. Government further acknowledges incarceration can have an impact on children and is therefore committed to improving the conditions in which children accompanying their mothers are accommodated, strengthening access to health and psychological services, and ensuring that their rights under the Convention on the Rights of the Child are respected. The over-arching principle in that is that a child should never be punished for the conduct of a parent. The child's best interests, safe lead, development and right to family life remain the primary considerations. Thank you.

I'd like to respond to the aspect of the child-friendly processes and the aspect of recorded evidence. We appreciate that and report that there has been an on-going process of amending the Evidence Act 1960, which is a very old law from the colonial times. Part of the aspects that are being captured is on the possibility of having evidence that is recorded and admitted before the courts of law. That is a work in progress. There was also a comment in terms of the age of criminal responsibility. Right now, we do not have a concrete report to give in terms of the advancement or progress. Research is still being undertaken as part of the law-making process to identify the priorities of Ugandans in regard.

To this aspect.

I'd like to respond then to the chairperson's question in terms of how we are working with the local actors as well as the religious actors in terms of child justice. And just by way of background, in 2019, the government undertook a study through the Uganda Law Reform Commission on informal justice systems.

A few years ago, the Hague International Law Institute also carried out a study.

And it showed that the first point of contact for criminal matters is at the local, that over 90% of Ugandans first report to the local entities before they come to the formal justice system. So being cognizant of that, we have continuously continued to work to ensure that we bring this on board.

So.

Uganda's engagement with local and religious leaders is structurally embedded in our policies and is not just a community outreach programme. I will report on five distinct interlocking levels.

The first one is that of the local council courts, which are the first formal tier of child justice mechanisms. which comes into play through the Local Council Act, and it gives the elected local council village leaders from the local council one, two and three, it gives them formal judicial authority over child matters as courts of first instance. We have over 60,000 of these currently in Uganda. These are local leaders and they are elected and they are legally recognized as the first forum for the vast majority of child justice issues. They resolve petty offenses through mediation, family restoration, parental accountability, and community service before cases go to the foremost infrastructures, structures. The LC courts also investigate cases of child neglect and abuse, and they refer these cases to the formal intervention of probation officers.

And the child and family protection units.

The second one is that of religious leaders, and these are our institutional partners in diversion and rehabilitation. The inter-religious council of Uganda unites the Catholic Church, the Church of Uganda, the Orthodox Church, the Seventh Day churches, and the Uganda Muslim Supreme Council as the primary formal faith-based partner on child rights. Religious leaders are recognized under the diversion guidelines as community resources to whom diverted children can be referred. Religious leaders regularly serve as fit persons under the Children's Act, and they are formally appointed to supervise diverted children. The Catholic Church, through Caritas Uganda and the Diocese and Justice and Peace Commissions, provide chaplaincy in remand homes and the National Rehabilitation Center, family liaison for the detained children, and parish-level reintegration support. The Church of Uganda's 2,200 primary schools, they operate mandatory child protection policies with referral pathways to the probation function. The mosques networks and the Qadi courts under the Uganda Muslim Supreme Council engage on family matters, including custody and maintenance, directly affecting children's welfare. The third parameter is that of traditional and clan leaders, and these come in to provide support in terms of reintegration and prevention. The clan leaders and elders are central to two critical child justice functions. One, prevention, where they do mediation of family disputes, they enforce customary accountability for children who have caused harm, and they intervene in harmful practices, including child marriage. And the other aspect is reintegration, where acceptance by clan and elder community is often the decisive factor in whether a child exiting the rehabilitative school or remand home successfully reintegrates or is rejected and returns to risk. The Buganda Kingdom has undertaken specific child protection programs, including the Kabaka's initiative addressing child sacrifice. Alternative panels at the district level also routinely involve the local council leadership and cultural leaders in placement decisions for children exiting justice facilities. The fourth is the justice for children programme and the community justice programme, which is funded by the Government of Sweden. These train local and religious leaders as fit persons, they strengthen community referral pathways to formal protection structures and engage community leaders in welcoming children returning from detention, and this directly addresses the family and community rejection that is.

A primary resettlement barrier.

In Karamoja, we are glad to report where the formal justice infrastructure is thinnest and child vulnerability is the highest, the clan elders and traditional leaders are especially critical. They do this through managing the cattle raiding related violence. They support the NUSAFF program and they mediate child marriage cases where legislative approaches alone have been insufficient. We do acknowledge that local and religious leaders simultaneously serve as child protection partners, but also in some context, they transmit harmful practices like child marriage, which are conducted through cultural ceremonies and corporal punishment, which are sometimes endorsed. But we do continue to engage and are cognizant that engagement therefore requires transformation of these institutions' own practices alongside partnership. Systematic national data on the outcome of these cases is not yet centrally compiled, and we are working to strengthen this through the CW MIS under development.

Thank you.

So, thank you so much. I want to respond to questions raised by the gentleman. I think he has left. I don't know whether I should respond about the issues relating to the Uganda Child Helpline, how much publicity is provided to 116 in schools and communities. I'd like to mention that the Uganda Child Helpline remains one of our most trusted and institutionalized platforms for reporting cases of violence against children. GBV, and now as recently as this year, child labor. Uganda Child Helpline has handled over 40,726 cases in the past three years. Out of these, 399 have been taken to court. 1,219 victims have received health services. 189 have received psychosocial services, psychosocial support services. We have done 20 community outreach programs. and been to over 120 schools in the past three years. The helpline also runs media campaigns periodically with support from development partners. They have a huge presence online. They have offline services, but they also have an AI chatbot, which we developed last year, which provides free mental health and psychosocial support using the SMS platform. We also have posters which we distribute in community places to enable people to call, and we regularly host community radio talk shows and community engagements where they popularize the 116 helpline as a toll-free line to report and respond to cases of violence against children, GBV, and child labor in communities. Iana Chevech asked about how many districts have the children reference groups. We have 30 districts having the children reference groups. I'll share with the committee the list of these districts and Kampala Capital City Authority. So we have 30 districts and one city. One of the major policy changes that the children reference groups have proposed or have delivered is one, having a child representative at the district child wellbeing committee and one child representative at the inter-ministerial child wellbeing committee. Our national child policy did not put a provision for child representative at these technical committees, and this was proposed and accepted as a policy change by the government of Uganda. I'm going to go deeply into a number of questions which were raised yesterday from health concerning routine immunization. The government of Uganda has continued to strengthen routine immunization. And during the past financial year, we implemented a big catch-up exercise vaccination campaign to identify and vaccinate children who had missed routine vaccinations. Our performance has improved considerably. DPT3, Hib, and Hepatitis B3 coverage has reached 97% against the national target of 100%. MRO1 coverage has reached 97% compared with the previous year of 94%. And our national DPT1 and DPT3 dropout rate, which was 3%, is still within the limit of the WHO acceptable range. However, we note that at least 20 districts out of the 146 record DPT3 coverage, which is below our 90% target. So government continues to use community-based defaulter tracing, catch-up vaccination, voluntary health teams, CSOs, and strengthen school and community mobilization to reach zero-dose children. Regarding the polio resurgence, Uganda recognizes that the polio events demonstrate the importance of maintaining high population immunity, sensitive surveillance, and rapid outbreak response, even when routine immunization coverage is nationally high. Uganda's response is to strengthen routine immunization identification and vaccination of zero dose under immunized children, conducting supplementary catch-up immunization where immunization gaps identified, strengthening community-based disease surveillance, monitoring rapid outbreak investigation and response, and strengthening cross-border surveillance and coordination. Under health financing, government of Uganda recognizes the committee's concern regarding health financing In the last financial year, the health sector on budget resource envelope was approximately 4 trillion, and government contributed over 68% of this. 31% came from development partners, and the health allocation represented only 5.6% of the national budget. Government's domestic contribution increased, however, this financial year by approximately 6% compared to the previous financial year. A number of financing challenges have been identified according to the annual health sector performance report for last year. Competing national priorities and fiscal constraints, declining external assistance, inadequate financing for medicine and supplies, delays in donor-funded procurement and implementation, and the need to raise domestic financing. Under the health service workforce, this is the current situation. The number of registered doctors increased in the past year from 9,388 to 10,433. Registered nurses and midwives increased from 119,132 to 133,542. The health worker density indicator reached 31.3 health workers per 10,000 population, exceeding the annual target of 25 per 10,000 population. However, we acknowledge a major remaining challenge, which is staffing of public health facilities with staffing rates of below 50%. So the report notes the following interventions that are currently being implemented by government of Uganda, improving the remuneration structure, increasing recruitment, deployment of medical interns, improving the human resource information system to ensure adequate human resource planning and prioritizing critical carders and underserved areas. Government has also expanded and upgraded the health facility infrastructure network. Last financial year, our health infrastructure was as follows. We have 3,612 health center threes, 262 health center fours, 189 general hospitals, 17 regional referral hospitals, eight national referral hospitals, alongside health center tools. How do we monitor health facility quality? We have a health facility quality assessment program, which has shown consistent improvement. Overall quality assessment performance increased from 63.8 in 2024 to 67.2 in 2025. However, we also acknowledge that a number of facilities do not yet meet universal acceptable standards. The facility readiness indicator was 65. 2 against a target of 80% and our health infrastructure recorded 74. 6. While our human resource recorded 62. 4 in the facility quality assessment. Government is therefore continuing to upgrade health facilities. Construct and rehabilitate new facilities. Equipping facilities. We will mention deeply in our report about the a neonatal intensive care units that have been established to improve neonatal health in all regional referral hospitals, recruitment of staff for the upgraded facilities, and improving availability of medicines and supplies. I will also respond to a question regarding the ECD centers. And how do we maintain standards? And how about families that can't afford? Uganda has categorized the ECD centers under four categories. We have daycare facilities for children below three, nursery schools that are privately owned, we have community-based centers that are run by faith-based institutions, and CSOs and home-based facilities. All these are part of our ECD programs. that provide early learning to children. So for children who are living in hard to reach areas, where it's not profitable to establish ECD centers, the current ECCE policy has proposed to provide resources for government to establish facilities for pre-primary education. Training ECD teachers already started five years ago. Annually, government trains at least 100 teachers and deploys them in these areas. So these centers are going to be served first by those that will be established by government, but also by CSOs and religious institutions. Community-based ECD centers are not subject to any taxes and receive incentives from government in terms of leading, reading, learning materials, and teacher capacity building. Uganda last year established the basic requirements and minimum standards for pre-primary education for children three to five years, and these standards are being rolled out. Training for school inspectors has already been undertaken and the monitoring system is put in place. For families that cannot afford, they benefit from existing livelihood programs to increase their incomes and ensure that children in these areas can afford, are reached with the services. For children living in refugee settlements, free pre-primary schools are provided for them to access pre-primary education. These ones are run in collaboration with the UNICEF, UNHCR, and the head of the education cluster in the humanitarian settings. And all these fit under the Education Response Plan 2 for Uganda. Families are informed about the importance of early learning through our parenting education programs. Our national parenting manual includes a particular session on supporting early learning straight from the home up to all levels of education. But also our key family care practices have a session number of areas supporting early learning from the home, including demonstrations on making play materials and interacting or early stimulation for children below three years. The number of schools that are inclusive, I'll leave that to my Minister. There's a question which was raised by Mr. Benoit on on children who are removed from streets and disappeared. I'd like to put it on record that government of Uganda has not received any report concerning children who have been rescued from the streets and have disappeared. Children who are removed from the streets are taken to a known location, which is Masulita Children's Village, where they are rehabilitated, provided with free health services, free accommodation, Case management for all these children is undertaken by trained probation and social welfare officers. Reintegration plans developed and implemented. Children who prefer to return to school are returned to schools within their district local governments. We're having 90% of children who are rescued from the streets coming from Karamoja. They are put in a boarding school in Napak District local government. and provided with meals, accommodation, and all scholastic materials at the expense of government. For those whose parents have been identified, they are reunited. For those who prefer to go into vocational training institutions, they are admitted at Koblenz Youth Skills Training Center, where they receive all these skills that they require. For children who are staying in homes that are not approved, Government of Uganda implements the approved children home rules, which detail the minimum requirements for establishment, for licensing and registration of an approved children's home, but also details the number of children and capacities for each children home and the particular categories of children that are supposed to be received in that children home. Admission to a children home is by way of an order from court but also maintenance and supervision is done by an independent Authority the probation and social welfare officers who are based at the district level monitor compliance to the regulations and to the registration that is issued by the minister of state for youth and children Affairs all children homes are supposed to submit biannual reports to the Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development, which are used to assess their compliance with existing regulations and service delivery standards. Financing for children homes is a bit restrictive. Government only provides technical support through training and provision of materials. During the COVID-19 pandemic, government of Uganda distributed food and non-food items to all approved children homes and those that were unapproved to cater for the deficiencies that resulted from the limited financial inflows from philanthropies and CSOs that were supporting these children homes. Post COVID-19, apart from free health services, free training and capacity building for the workers, monitoring and support supervision and regulation, there is no support that is provided to these children. However, linkages to education, to free pre-primary education, to free primary education and secondary education is available. And as recently as this year, all children homes catering for children with special needs will benefit from the child disability benefit that has been launched by government of Uganda. Over to you, honorable minister.

Thank you, honorable minister. Madam chair and members of the committee. In the interest of time, I will quickly answer the question on how government ensures that the budget allocated for programs targeted at the rights of the child and how those resources are spent to translate into measurable outcomes and how they are tracked. We wish to reiterate the following. The management of public resources in Uganda is anchored in the Public Finance Management Act 2015, which establishes the principles and procedures for sound fiscal policy. orderly public expenditure and accountability in the use of government funds. The Act further obliges all government entities to mainstream gender and equity considerations in their budgetary processes, thereby making every allocation not only an expenditure item, but a measurable commitment to inclusive service delivery and the welfare of all Ugandans, including children. Central to this architecture is the statutory role of the Equal Opportunities Commission, established under the Equal Opportunities Commission Act, pursuant to Article 32 of the Constitution of the Republic of Uganda. Before any budget is approved and funds are released, the EOC, Equal Opportunities Commission, assesses the national budget estimates and ministerial policy statements for gender and equity responsiveness and issues a certificate of gender and equity compliance. Important to note is that this certificate is a precondition for budget appropriation. The issuance of that certificate of, sorry, the issuance of the certificate of compliance guarantees that the government is able to track expenditure and ensure value for money in allocations meant to take care of children. To monitor budget performance, reports are submitted quarterly and these inform subsequent disbursements. This means that programs for the welfare of children, which have been elaborated earlier by my distinguished colleague, are not only protected at the approval stage, but are continuously monitored, verified, and refined throughout the financial year, guaranteeing accountability, value for money, and the effective delivery of service to the children of Uganda. I thank you. Honorable Minister, back to you. Thank you.

Thank you. Thank you, Chair. I will address myself just three issues or questions. The first was a question on what happens if there is a language barrier for refugee children in schools in settlements. I wish to inform the committee translation services are provided as a protection tool through implementation partners of the UNHCR. You recall we mentioned the challenges faced by resources. These are some of the key issues that require funding, considering the additional cost to the host country, which does not have the requisite capacities and skills to support this. So in summary, UNHCR recruits and pays partners to provide that service. The second question I want to respond to regarding the children in armed conflict and civilians tried in a court martial. Chair, I would like to inform that civilians are not tried in a court martial in Uganda. Secondly, Uganda is peaceful and secure. And as we know, children in armed conflicts are found globally across multiple regions, primarily within active war zones. Uganda doesn't fit in that category, and as such, we don't have any child soldiers. In fact, what we are actively involved in is to support mediation efforts in our own region for peace and security. We are also involved in stabilization activities. As you may be aware, for instance, We are involved in activities to support stabilization in Somalia and also in the DRC, working collaboratively with the concerned country to neutralize negative forces who recruit and, of course, lure children within their ranks. This is done often at very high sacrifice by our own forces. The third issue and question I would like to address is the issue of the Anti-Homosexuality Act. This was something that we touched on yesterday, but I just want to make a comment and respond since it was raised again. A comment was made that it's the worst of all acts, and a call has been made to repeal the law, and they're sorry for many young people in Uganda. I would like to say this, Chair. Again, a campaign was unearthed in Uganda targeting children in schools in the entire country. How was it discovered? It was discovered because children resisted going to school, and questions arose, why were kids not wanting to go to school? What was found out was that there was promotion use of audio, video, and books in schools. When it was found out, this was unacceptable. And across the country, across the political divide, across religious ethnic groups, there was a call demanding for action. In Uganda, promotion of any sexuality, heterosexual or homosexual, is unacceptable. These are our norms, these are our cultures, and these are our beliefs. As a result of what was unearthed, Parliament, which has a responsibility to legislate, like in many of the countries represented here, through a consultation process, adopted a bill which went through and eventually was enacted into law. The bill does not discriminate. What the bill prohibits is promotion of any kind, and I will repeat it, promotion of any kind, heterosexuality or homosexuality. This is a matter that we have engaged with international partners, and Uganda has, as part of the culture, we respect people's values. We respect people's norms. What we find intolerable is an attempt to impose values that are not ours. So what we expect from others is to respect our own cultures and our norms. This bill, as far as we are concerned, protects children. They are in a happier place. Our children are well. And as we speak now, the bill continues to receive support from the country. And just to add, It does not discriminate in terms of access to social services, whether it is education, whether it is health, et cetera. And we have often said it would challenge anyone who would say that it discriminates on any Ugandan based on their sexuality. I would like to thank you, Chair.

Honourable Minister, I will respond to questions on birth registration. Uganda recognizes that birth registration is the gateway to identity, protection, and access to essential services, and does not make a distinction between children born in or out of wedlock. Uganda has made progress in expanding birth registration. The National Identification and Registration Authority has scaled up the electronic birth registration system and mobile vital record system with support from partners. and has such reached out to underserved districts and integrated birth registration with immunization services in over 120 districts. To raise awareness on the need for birth registration, they have made use of what they call birth registration weeks that are held in districts, including those in hard to reach areas, such as Arua, Moroto, Mayuge, and other places, which have registered over 600,000 children registered between the years 2021 and 2023. In the financial year 2024 and 2025, the National Identification and Registration Authority registered 498,596 births and a total of 357 birth notifications were received from health facilities and communities where births took place. In that financial year alone, NIRA, which is the National Registration Authority, registered a total of 1,231,369 children aged between the ages of 0 to 9 years. Of that category, 609,345 were male, while 622,015 were females. NIRA also registered a total of 3,972,940 children aged between the ages of 10 to 17, with 1.9 million being male and 2 million are females. NIRA also registered births in refugee settlements and recorded 25,134 new births in 2024 alone, ensuring that recognition and protection of children born in displacement as well. So with that, thank you very much, Chair.

Let me just add a little more on pre-primary education that my colleague earlier on had Historically, the government of Uganda has not directly funded pre-primary operations, leaving early childhood education to private providers, parents and NGOs. With the launch of the early childhood care and education policy, the state has introduced its first targeted fiscal framework. Under total policy allocation, the government has committed 19.74 billion shillings over a rolling five-year timeline, specifically for early childhood care and education system building and regulatory rollouts. That is establishing public centers exclusively in underserved rural parishes where private sectors do not operate, and funding the professionalization and curriculum training of early grade caregivers and strengthening. quality assurance. And by December 2025, however, we had 24,923 registered pre-primary schools with 592,049 learners, of which 11,713 were learners with special needs, 18,790 teachers and PTR of 31 to 1. Also key to note is that for those areas where parents cannot afford, government doesn't work alone. Government works hand in hand in collaboration with NGOs, with CSOs, with religious institutions to establish community-based ECD centers so to ensure that even in the smallest of units, children are not completely left out. And in response to inclusive Earlier on, you wanted the numbers of some of the schools that are registered. At primary level, we have 27 schools that are registered, and at secondary level, we have 26 schools where they have teachers who are trained to handle even children with special needs. and equipment installed in all these institutions and with all the relevant aids that they need to ensure that children with disabilities are incorporated. And to answer the question on malaria, I would like to bring to your notice that Uganda is driving a major nationwide campaign and a strategic plan to eliminate malaria completely by 2030. And we are shifting the focus from just control to complete eradication of malaria. Key to note is that there are national strategies that have been put in place and the National Malaria Elimination Strategic Plan spanning from 2026 up to 2030. It was launched in April this year, 2026. And also maybe to bring it to your attention, I am a legislator in the Parliament of Uganda and on the 26th of July 2026, we had our annual parliamentary malaria the walk. So the legislators are coming out and we are taking the lead to end malaria by 2030. The Deputy Speaker of Parliament this year was the chief walker alongside other legislators, diplomats, civil society groups, and the theme was walking the talk and end malaria now. So we are committed to this fight against malaria. The question of us to how effective the net distribution is. I already told you earlier on that the ministry has what we call the village health teams that work.

Two in every village.

And recently, like I said, it's being reinforced by the community health extension workers that was also recently launched to help and they aid in the distribution household to household, door to door campaigns. This is their everyday work. So that is some of them. And also the malaria, the mosquito net distribution was launched recently also. We have about 25.8 million in April this year. Mosquito nets were launched to be distributed to 130 districts. That is already also in the fight against malaria. And in conclusion, I know that there was a question raised on Ebola and wanted to know the impact that the recent Ebola outbreak had. Yes, we had an outbreak on the 15th of May 2026, and I'm happy to report that Uganda successfully halted the transmission. And of those affected, all the cases to note in Uganda were imported adults from the Democratic Republic of Congo who were coming into Uganda to seek care. And only one child was infected by the mother, and they all recovered. The health workers, the four health workers who also were affected, had very minimal interaction with children. So I welcome your congratulatory message where WHO declared Uganda Ebola-free. And now I also take the floor to invite you to feel free to come to Uganda now. You know, Uganda is the Pearl of Africa. It's a tourist destination. Don't be scared. We'll be ready and willing to receive you anytime. I thank you.
Thank you very much. Now I would like to give floor back to the coordinator of the country task force, Mr. Ben Romain Kirespo.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Madam Minister, Excellencies, distinguished member of the delegation of the Republic of Uganda, as we bring this intense and highly productive dialogue to a close, I want to express on behalf of the task force, but also on the entire committee, my gratitude to the high-level multi-sectorial delegation of Uganda for your active and dedicated participation to our exchange. Our exchange over the past two days has been characterized by a truly constructive, transparent and collaborative spirit, reflecting our shared commitment to the advancement of children's rights. We highly appreciate your detailed response to almost all our questions. We must warmly congratulate the Government of Uganda for your constitution that embeds some of the rights of the Convention, the comprehensive amended Children's Act, the numerous national strategies, the very significant progress engranged in several key areas since our last review. For example, when it comes to child survival and health, the decline in under-five mortality, the reduction of child stunting rates. Your commitment to diversion and restorative justice is highly commendable. We also praise the development of the child wellbeing management information system to address critical child data gaps. It seems to be promising. The very fact that you sent your report and took part in this review is a clear sign of your continued commitment. We thank you for that. We know that the path for the full realization of the Convention is an ongoing journey, and we encourage you to redouble your efforts in addressing several persistent challenges. You have recognized this yourself. We know, for instance, that the global ban on corporal punishment in all settings is not yet achieved. Also, the legal ban is not sufficient. There is a need to convince the population, uh, of the detrimental effect of using violence in education, and we need to change the mentality promoting positive education. Let us not forget all the children living in vulnerable situations: children in street situations, minorities and indigenous groups, refugees and migrant children in institutions, children living in poverty, working children, among many others. We understand that the State cannot cover from one day to another all domains covered by the Convention and need the support of the international community, especially in some specific policies. We duly noted that the considerable cuts in international cooperation have put you under huge constraint, and we deeply deplore this evolution. In the meantime, we would really want the country to be able to cover progressively the budget that are needed to implement the Convention from your own budget. As I said in my introductory message, we also had to address very sensitive issues, in particular when it comes to the safeguard of the vital space of civil society and the child right defenders, ensuring that the Non-Governmental Organization Act and the newly enacted Protection of Sovereignty Act do not restrict their legitimate advocacy. We have also raised our grave concern about the consequences of the Anti-Homosexual Act. Our concern do not intend to interfere with the values of Uganda, but to uphold the rights of all children, no matter their sexual orientation and gender identity. We expressly call on Ugandan government to resist the global trend towards rolling back protection for fundamental rights, particularly those of children, which is regrettably becoming increasingly prevalent. Looking ahead, the concluding observation we will adopt at the end of this session should be seen as a strategic roadmap to guide Uganda's national plan and budgetary allocation over the coming years. To ensure a robust and effective follow-up, we strongly recommend that Uganda strengthen its inter-ministerial committee on human rights, providing it with the necessary mandate and financial resources to systematically track and coordinate the implementation of these treaty obligations. Furthermore, we emphasize the importance of disseminating these concluding observations widely, and we urge you to produce and distribute a child-friendly version, including in local language, so that children themselves, including those in the most marginalized and rural communities, can understand and claim their rights. We would like to see children involved in the implementation of these concluding observations. We leave this session confident that the Republic of Uganda will translate the commitments made during this dialogue in concrete, lasting action on the ground. The Committee stands ready to accompany and support you in this noble task. I thank you, and I wish you a safe journey back to Kampala.
Thank you. I would like to give the floor back to Your Excellency for the concluding remarks.

Madam Chairperson, members of the Committee, ladies and gentlemen, we came here in a spirit of sincerity and openness to share with the Committee the journey we have taken on implementing the Convention on the Rights of the Child. On behalf of the Government of the Republic of Uganda, I wish to express our sincere appreciation to the Committee for the constructive dialogue and engagement during the last two days. Children are dependents who represent the future foundation of any society, including our own. Fulfilling our obligations has taken centre stage, and as we have demonstrated, significant milestones have been achieved in implementing the Convention, although some work remains to be done. In this regard, I wish to reaffirm our unwavering commitment to fulfilling our obligations under the Convention on the Rights of the Child and its Optional Protocols. Uganda remains particularly committed to advancing education accessible and quality health services, comprehensive child protection systems, social protection measures, a child-sensitive juvenile justice framework, and the prevention of all forms of violence, exploitation and discrimination. The Committee's observations and concerns relating to children with disabilities education, health, social protection, child labor, children in street situations, juvenile justice, and violence against children, among others, are noted and appreciated. And if there are other questions or concerns that we're not responding to, we shall do so in writing. We'll continue on our path to strengthen national efforts to ensure that every child, regardless of background, ability or circumstance can enjoy their full rights, reach their full potential to ensure that no child is left behind. I thank you.

Your Excellency, Madam Minister, Your Excellency, Mr. Ambassador, distinguished members of the delegation, I thank you very much for these two constructive days and constructive dialogue with clear answers you have provided. And you are already aware that you have 48 hours after this dialogue to provide your information in written. We will very much appreciate it. We understand that this was a lot of, a big amount of questions, which also explains the very important constructive dialogue and your answers provided also, which triggered more questions from the side of the committee members. We appreciate and commend all the positive developments Uganda has proven as positive developments for the children of Uganda, for all the vulnerable groups you mentioned during these two days. We commend, once again, appreciate it, but you also aware about the challenges you have. And I really appreciated your comment also recently now that you will take the recommendations done by the colleagues at the CRC and will try your best to address them and to implement intangible results on the ground. I fully understand you have your difficulties. It is not so easy to implement, despite the best intentions you have. It's very difficult to implement it in tangible results for children. So you have our full support, and we hope that the next time when the Uganda delegation will come to the CRC, you will provide really excellent results for the children of Uganda, based hopefully on the concluding observations the committee. I thank you very much and please convey our warmest regards to all the children of Uganda. Thank you and wishing you safe travel back home. Thank you.
